headline: Argonne National Laboratory has shown an AI agent that takes plain-language instructions and steers an X-ray microscope to a chosen spot in a microchip.
score_reason: Pool score 5 lowered by 1: the demonstration dates from 5 Oct, and no performance comparison is given.
source: Argonne National Laboratory (as relayed by Streamlinefeed)
summary: Streamlinefeed, describing an Argonne National Laboratory release, reports that on 5 Oct 2026 the laboratory showed an AI agent finding the boundary between two regions of a microchip at an X-ray beamline after a plain-language request, by scanning, analysing images and moving to a closer look. It acts alone only on low-risk steps and asks for human approval otherwise, and the release gives no comparison of accuracy or time against human operators.
importance_line: Scientists who run costly beamlines could save effort, but the step is narrow, it is not a fully self-driving laboratory, and no speed or accuracy figures are given.
notes: The pool link (HPCwire) was blocked; the entry rests on Streamlinefeed's account of Argonne's own release. The microscope is steered by software, so machine_action is true only in the sense of an instrument moving.
